# Problem1
```{r}
library(tidyverse)
library(p8105.datasets)
library(patchwork)
data("ny_noaa")
```

```{r}
ny_noaa |>
  summarise(
    across(
      everything(),
      ~sum(is.na(.x))
    )
  )
ny_noaa|>
  summarise(
    across(
      everything(),
      ~mean(is.na(.x))*100
    )
  )
```

This dataset contains daily weather observations from weather stations across New York State from January 1, 1981, through December 31, 2010. It contains station identifiers(`id`), observation dates(`date`), precipitation(`prcp`), snowfall(`snow`), snow depth(`snwd`), maximum temperature(`tmax`), and minimum temperature(`tmin`). The dataset contains `r nrow(ny_noaa)` observations and `r ncol(ny_noaa)` variables.

Missingness varies across variables. The station ID and date have no missing values. Precipitation has relatively little missing data (5.62%), while snowfall and snow depth have 14.7% and 22.8% missing, respectively. Maximum and minimum temperatures have the highest missingness, at approximately 43.7% each.


```{r}
ny_noaa_clean = 
  ny_noaa|>
  separate(
    date,
    into = c("year","month","day"),
    sep = "-"
  )|>
  mutate(
    year = as.integer(year),
    month = as.integer(month),
    day = as.integer(day),
    prcp = as.numeric(prcp)/10,
    snow = as.numeric(snow)/10,
    snwd = as.numeric(snwd)/10,
    tmax = as.numeric(tmax)/10,
    tmin = as.numeric(tmin)/10
  )
```

I converted year, month, and day to integer, precipitation, snowfall, and snow depth to centimeters, and maximum and minimum temperature to degrees Celsius.


```{r}
ny_noaa_clean|>
  filter(!is.na(snow))|>
  count(snow, sort = T)|>
  slice_head(n=10)
```

The most common snowfall value is 0, because snowfall does not occur on most observation days.


```{r}
temp_by_station = 
  ny_noaa_clean|>
  filter(month ==1|month ==7)|>
  group_by(id, year, month)|>
  summarise(
    mean_tmax = mean(tmax, na.rm = T),
    .groups = "drop"
  )

ggplot(temp_by_station,
       aes(x = year, y = mean_tmax, group = id))+
  geom_line(alpha=0.3)+
  facet_grid(. ~ month)+
  labs(
    title = "Average Maximum Temperature in January and July",
    x = "Year",
    y = "Average Maximum Temperature"
  ) +
  theme_minimal()
```

Average maximum temperatures are generally high in July than in January, reflecting seasonal differences. Temperatures vary across stations and years. A few potential outliers are observed, including January temperatures below -10°C and July temperatures as low as approximately 15°C, which are substantially lower than those at other stations.


```{r}
p1 = 
  ggplot(
    ny_noaa_clean,
    aes(x=tmin,y=tmax)
  )+
  geom_bin2d()+
  labs(
    title = "Maximum vs Minimum Temperature",
    x = "Minimum Temperature (°C)",
    y = "Maximum Temperature (°C)"
  )+
  theme_minimal()

snow_by_year = 
  ny_noaa_clean|>
  filter(snow>0, snow<100)
p2 = 
  ggplot(
    snow_by_year,
    aes(x=factor(year),y=snow)
  )+
  geom_boxplot()+
  labs(
    title = "Distribution of snowfall by year",
    x = "Year",
    y = "Snowfall (cm)"
  )+
  theme_minimal()+
  theme(
    axis.text.x = element_text(
      angle = 90,
      hjust = 1
    )
  )

p1 + p2
```

Maximum and minimum temperatures show a positive relationship. Most observations are concentrated in the central region, while some extreme values are present. Some extreme values, such as temperatures of 60°C recorded at one station on multiple consecutive days, may indicate potential data quality issues.

snowfall distributions are generally similar across years, with relatively low medians. Many high outliers are present in each year, with some observations exceeding 50cm. Although the maximum snowfall values vary across years, there is no clear overall trend in the distributions over time.


# Problem2

```{r}
covar =
  read.csv("data/nhanes_covar.csv", skip = 4)|>
  janitor::clean_names()
accel = 
  read.csv("data/nhanes_accel.csv")|>
  janitor::clean_names()

nhanes = covar |>
  inner_join(accel, by = "seqn")|>
  filter(age>=21)|>
  drop_na(sex, age, bmi, education)|>
  mutate(
    sex = factor(
      sex,
      levels = c(1,2),
      labels = c("male","female")
    ),
    education = factor(
      education,
      levels = c(1,2,3),
      labels = c("Less than high school","High school equivalent","More than high school")
    )
  )
```


```{r}
sex_education_table = nhanes|>
  count(education, sex, name = "n")|>
  pivot_wider(
    names_from = sex,
    values_from = n,
    values_fill = 0
  )|>
  rename(
    `Education level` = education,
    Men = male,
    Women = female
  )|>
  mutate(Total = Men + Women)
```

The number of men and women are similar in less than high school and more than high school groups. In the high school equivalent group, there are more men (n=35) than women (n-23).

```{r}
nhanes|>
  ggplot(aes(x=age,fill=sex,color=sex))+
  geom_density(alpha = 0.30, linewidth = 0.7)+
  facet_wrap(~education, nrow = 1)+
  labs(
    title = "Age distributions by sex and education level",
    x = "Age",
    y = "Density",
    fill = "Sex",
    color = "Sex"
  )
```

The age distributions differed by sex within some education groups. Among participants with less than a high school education, the age distributions of men and women overlapped substantially, with relatively high density around ages 60-75. In the high school equivalent group, women tended to be concentrated at older ages, with a peak around age 70, whereas men showed a broader and more variable age distribution. In the more than high school group, both sexes were concentrated at younger ages, especially around age 30; the female distribution was more sharply peaked, while the male distribution was more spread out and showed a smaller second peak at older ages.


```{r}
nhanes = 
  nhanes |>
  mutate(
    total_activity = rowSums(
      across(min1:min1440),
      na.rm = T
    )
  )

nhanes|>
  ggplot(aes(x = age, y = total_activity, color = sex))+
  geom_point(alpha = 0.5)+
  geom_smooth(se=F,linewidth = 1)+
  facet_wrap(~education)+
  labs(
    title = "Total daily activity by age, sex, and education",
    x = "Age",
    y = "Total daily MIMS",
    color = "Sex"
  )
```

Total daily activity generally decreased with age, although the pattern varied by education level and sex. In the less than high school group, both men and women showed an overall decline in total activity as age increased. Female activity was higher at younger ages, while the male smooth showed a temporary increase around ages 55–60 before declining. In the high school equivalent group, women had higher predicted total activity than men at approximately ages 30–50, with a peak around age 40. For both sexes, total activity generally declined at older ages, although the female trend was more variable. In the more than high school group, women had relatively stable activity levels until approximately age 60, followed by a noticeable decline. Men showed a more gradual decline in activity across age.

```{r}
activity=
  nhanes|>
  pivot_longer(
    cols = min1:min1440,
    names_to = "minute",
    names_prefix = "min",
    names_transform = list(minute = as.integer),
    values_to = "mims"
  )|>
  mutate(
    minute = minute - 1,
    hour = minute / 60
  )|>
  group_by(education,sex,minute,hour)|>
  summarise(
    mean_mims = mean(mims, na.rm = T),
    .groups = "drop"
  )

activity|>
  ggplot(aes(x = hour, y = mean_mims, color = sex)) +
  geom_line(alpha = 0.65, linewidth = 0.45) +
  geom_smooth(se = F, span = 0.10, linewidth = 1)+
  facet_wrap(~education, nrow =1)+
  scale_x_continuous(
    breaks = seq(0,24,by = 4),
    limits = c(0,24)
  )+
  labs(
    title = "Mean 24-hour activity profiles by education and sex",
    x = "Time of day",
    y = "Mean MIMS",
    color = "Sex"
  )
```

Across all three education groups, mean activity followed a similar daily pattern: activity was lowest during the early morning hours (approximately 2–5 AM), increased rapidly after approximately 6 AM, remained relatively high during the daytime, and declined again in the late evening.

Sex differences varied across education levels. Among participants with less than a high school education, men had slightly higher mean activity during the nighttime and early-morning hours, whereas women showed a somewhat higher peak in late morning. In the high school equivalent group, women generally had higher mean activity than men from the morning through early afternoon, although the two curves became more similar later in the day. In the more than high school group, women had consistently higher mean activity than men for most daytime hours.

Overall, the figure suggests that daily activity patterns are similar in timing across education groups, but the magnitude of activity and the difference between men and women may vary by education level.
